items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a permanent or semi-permanent change of residence, usually for at least a year”.
items.answer: Migration

items.stem: Explain why the distinction between voluntary and forced migration is not always clear.
items.answer: Many migrants are pushed by poverty, drought or insecurity yet choose when and where to move; environmental degradation can make staying impossible gradually; decisions are made within constraints.

items.stem: Explain why migration is difficult to define and measure.
items.answer: Different time thresholds (one year), undocumented migration, circulation that is not recorded, internal moves not registered, changing borders.

items.stem: With the help of examples, evaluate the claim that classifying migration as either voluntary or forced is of little value.
items.answer: For: Many moves combine choice and compulsion (drought-driven migration from the Sahel; economic collapse in Venezuela); the line is blurred. Against: The distinction matters legally (refugee status under the 1951 Convention), for aid and for understanding causes and impacts; extreme cases (Syria, Ukraine) are clearly forced. Conclusion: Migration is better seen as a continuum, but the classification remains useful for policy and law.

items.answer: Correct. By definition a refugee has crossed an international border; those who have not are IDPs.

items.stem: Distinguish between internal and international migration, with examples.
items.answer: Internal: within a country, e.g. rural-urban migration to Lagos. International: across national borders, e.g. Mexicans to the USA.

items.stem: Explain Lee’s model of migration.
items.answer: Origin and destination each have positive, negative and neutral factors perceived differently by individuals; intervening obstacles (distance, cost, laws) lie between; personal factors (age, education, family) affect the decision; migration is selective.

items.stem: Explain why migration is often selective by age.
items.answer: Young adults have fewest ties, most to gain from new jobs and education, and can adapt; older people have property and family commitments.

items.stem: Assess the view that economic factors are the main cause of migration. In your answer you may refer to refugees and intervening obstacles.
items.answer: For: Most voluntary migrants seek higher wages and jobs (South Asians to the Gulf, Mexicans to the USA); remittances support families. Against: Conflict and persecution (Syria, Sudan), environmental hazards, family reunification, education, retirement and lifestyle also cause migration; intervening obstacles and personal factors shape decisions. Conclusion: Economic factors explain the largest share of voluntary migration, but forced and social migration are important and decisions combine many factors.

items.stem: Explain why migration is more important than natural increase for population change in some countries.
items.answer: Very low fertility gives little natural increase (Germany, Italy) so immigration determines growth; in Gulf states labour immigration dominates; emigration causes decline in Eastern Europe or Pacific islands.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per developed example [3]

items.stem: Explain how migration affects the age-sex structure of source and destination areas.
items.answer: Migrants are mainly young adults (often male), so destinations gain working-age people and source areas lose them, leaving older people and children; this alters future birth rates.

items.stem: “Migration is now more important than natural increase in causing population change.” Discuss. In your answer you may refer to age structure and fertility.
items.answer: For: In HICs with low fertility (Germany, Canada, UK) immigration accounts for most growth; Gulf states; emigration causes decline in Bulgaria, Latvia, Puerto Rico. Against: Globally migration does not change world population; in high-fertility LICs (Niger, DRC, Pakistan) natural increase dominates; migration effects vary by scale. Conclusion: Migration dominates in many HICs and at local scales, but natural increase remains the main driver of growth globally and in LICs.

items.stem: Grace argues that migration is now more important than natural increase in causing population change. How far do you agree? Support your answer with examples. In your answer you may refer to fertility, scale and age structure.
items.answer: For: In HICs with low fertility (Germany, Canada, UK) immigration accounts for most growth; Gulf states; emigration causes decline in Bulgaria, Latvia, Puerto Rico. Against: Globally migration does not change world population; in high-fertility LICs (Niger, DRC, Pakistan) natural increase dominates; migration effects vary by scale. Conclusion: Migration dominates in many HICs and at local scales, but natural increase remains the main driver of growth globally and in LICs.

items.answer: Voluntary, international (skilled, possibly permanent)

items.stem: Classify each movement (voluntary or forced; temporary or permanent; internal or international) and give a reason for one of your answers. (a) A nurse from the Philippines takes a three-year contract in a hospital in Riyadh. (b) A retired couple from Manchester moves to the Algarve in Portugal. items.answer: (a) voluntary, temporary, international. (b) voluntary, permanent, international (retirement). (c) forced, permanent, internal (displacement).

items.stem: Country R had a population of 60 million, a crude birth rate of 16 per 1000 and a crude death rate of 9 per 1000. In the same year 416 000 people immigrated and 609 000 emigrated. Calculate the net migration and the net migration rate per 1000.

Town O has a population of 120 thousand. items.stem: “Classifying migration as either voluntary or forced is of little value.” Discuss. In your answer you may refer to refugees and law.
items.answer: For: Many moves combine choice and compulsion (drought-driven migration from the Sahel; economic collapse in Venezuela); the line is blurred. Against: The distinction matters legally (refugee status under the 1951 Convention), for aid and for understanding causes and impacts; extreme cases (Syria, Ukraine) are clearly forced. Conclusion: Migration is better seen as a continuum, but the classification remains useful for policy and law.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a barrier between origin and destination that makes migration more difficult, such as distance, cost, borders or immigration laws”.
items.answer: Intervening obstacle
items.markingKey: Intervening obstacle: a barrier between origin and destination that makes migration more difficult, such as distance, cost, borders or immigration laws. [1]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A student writes: “Push factors alone explain why people migrate.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain how improvements in transport and communications affect migration.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. Migration requires a destination with perceived advantages; pull factors, obstacles and personal factors also matter. (b) They reduce the cost and difficulty of moving (intervening obstacles), spread information about opportunities, and allow migrants to keep in touch, encouraging chain migration.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) [3]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why migration is often selective by age. (b) Explain Lee’s model of migration.
items.answer: (a) Young adults have fewest ties, most to gain from new jobs and education, and can adapt; older people have property and family commitments. (b) Origin and destination each have positive, negative and neutral factors perceived differently by individuals; intervening obstacles (distance, cost, laws) lie between; personal factors (age, education, family) affect the decision; migration is selective.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) 1 mark per element [4]

items.stem: A student surveyed migrants living in a city and recorded the number who had come from each of 10 source districts, together with the distance of each district from the city. Table 1.2 gives, for each district, the distance from the city (km) and the number of migrants surveyed. District 1: 89, 95. District 2: 201, 41. District 3: 224, 60. District 4: 231, 81. District 5: 239, 48. District 6: 265, 45. District 7: 293, 56. District 8: 394, 13. District 9: 399, 12. District 10: 421, 32. Critical values of rs for n = 10: 0.564 (0.05 level) and 0.745 (0.01 level). Suggest one limitation of the method and how the investigation could be improved.
items.answer: Districts differ in population size, so raw numbers are biased; express migrants per 10 000 population of each district and increase the sample size.
items.markingKey: 1 mark limitation; 1 mark improvement [2]

items.stem: A student surveyed migrants living in a city and recorded the number who had come from each of 11 source districts, together with the distance of each district from the city. Table 3.2 gives, for each district, the distance from the city (km) and the number of migrants surveyed. District 1: 41, 86. District 2: 152, 76. District 3: 188, 65. District 4: 198, 51. District 5: 212, 63. District 6: 296, 29. District 7: 321, 19. District 8: 343, 36. District 9: 401, 14. District 10: 419, 4. District 11: 423, 10. Critical values of rs for n = 11: 0.536 (0.05 level) and 0.709 (0.01 level). (a) State a suitable null hypothesis for this investigation. (b) Suggest reasons for the relationship shown by the data.
items.answer: (a) There is no relationship between the distance from the city (km) and the number of migrants surveyed. (b) Distance decay: cost, time and lack of information increase with distance, and nearer districts have stronger social links (chain migration), so more migrants come from nearby.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) 1 mark per developed reason [3]

items.stem: A revision website states: “Net migration can be negative even when many people are arriving.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. If more people leave than arrive, net migration is negative.
